title: Logistics stocks: how to analyze freight companies
description: Logistics stocks live on the freight cycle — Maersk EBIT fell 31→3.5bn USD in three years. How to read volume, yield and synergies — DSV worked through.
author: AK1A Research Lab
body:
Logistics stocks are shares in the companies that move the world's goods — shipping lines, freight forwarders and contract logisticians. The industry is an analysis world of its own for one single reason: demand for freight follows world trade, but the supply of ships, planes and trucks cannot be switched off and on in step. When trade grows faster than capacity, freight rates — and profitability — shoot upward; when new capacity arrives into a slowdown, they fall just as fast. Maersk, one of the world's largest container shipping lines, reported an operating result (EBIT) of 31 billion dollars in 2022 and 3.5 billion in 2025 — the same company, the same ships, one cycle.

This guide walks through the industry's three business models, the freight cycle worked through in numbers, how to read a forwarder's income statement — and what DSV's Schenker integration teaches about adjusted earnings.

## Three business models — what logistics stocks earn money on

Whoever analyzes logistics stocks begins by sorting the company into one of three bins, because the three carry different accounts. **The shipping line** owns its vessels (Maersk): revenue is freight rate times volume, and the cost side is a heavy and fixed apparatus — port fees, crew, financing — which gives a high operating leverage: earnings swing violently with the freight rate. **The forwarder** (DSV, Kuehne+Nagel) rarely owns the vehicle; the company buys capacity from shipping lines and airlines and resells transport, customs handling and solutions — capital intensity is lower, margins thinner and the cycle dampened. **Contract logistics** runs warehouses, packing and distribution for others on multi-year agreements — the most stable revenues and the strictest margins.

The weights are visible in DSV's segment report: of the group's EBIT before one-off items of 19.6 billion DKK in 2025, 13.0 billion came from Air & Sea — two thirds of the earnings from the division that buys and sells capacity at sea and in the air — while Road contributed 2.7 and Contract Logistics 3.8 billion.

## The freight cycle — the price is set at auction for cargo space

A freight rate is an auction: shippers bid for a limited number of cargo spaces, and the price lands where the last load just about pays. Supply is capacity — vessels in operation, actual sailing routes — and demand is volume: world trade, inventory goods, consumer goods. Maersk's last four years show the whole mechanism. 2022: revenue 82 billion dollars and EBIT 31 billion — an operating margin of 31 ÷ 82 = 37.8 percent, driven by the pandemic's trailing demand and full ships. 2023: newly delivered capacity met slowing trade, EBIT fell to around 4 billion — minus 87 percent in one year. 2024: the attacks in the Red Sea forced reroutes around Africa, which removed effective capacity and lifted freight rates — EBIT 6.5 billion. 2025: normalized routes and softer volume, EBIT 3.5 billion on almost unchanged revenue of 54 billion — the margin 3.5 ÷ 54.0 = 6.5 percent.

Note what the series teaches: revenue was essentially flat 2024–2025 while the earnings nearly halved. In cyclical industries the operating margin is the barometer, and [cycle risk](/kurser/rk-05-cykelrisk) begins precisely in that insight.

## The forwarder — read gross profit, not revenue

A forwarder's revenue has a double nature: when the transport is reported as principal, the purchased freight sits in revenue, and when freight rates rise the revenue swells mechanically without the company having sold a single transport more. Gross profit — revenue minus purchased freight — is therefore the forwarder's true revenue line. DSV 2025: revenue 247.3 billion DKK (167.1 billion in 2024, after the Schenker acquisition), gross profit 66.9 billion — a gross margin of 66,859 ÷ 247,331 = 27.0 percent against 25.7 the year before — and EBIT before one-off items 19.6 billion, an improvement of 19,611 ÷ 16,096 − 1 = 21.8 percent.

The contrast gives the market position: Kuehne+Nagel, which has grown organically, reported 2025 net sales of 24.5 billion CHF, gross profit 8.8 billion (36.0 percent) and EBIT 1,242 million CHF — down 24.9 percent from 2024, with an operating margin of 1,242 ÷ 24,476 = 5.1 percent. DSV's +21.8 percent is acquisition; Kuehne+Nagel's −24.9 percent is the market. The difference between organic and acquired growth is [an analysis in itself](/kurser/tx-01-organisk-mot-forvarvad-tillvaxt).

## The acquisition machine — read both earnings lines

DSV is the industry's most consistent acquirer, and the Schenker year 2025 is a lesson in reading two lines at once. EBIT before one-off items rose 21.8 percent — but profit from continuing operations fell from 10.2 to 8.5 billion DKK, minus 16.8 percent, because integration costs of 4.5 billion were booked as one-off items. Diluted adjusted earnings per share became 50.9 DKK against 51.6 — essentially unchanged although revenue grew 48 percent: the purchase was partly paid with own shares, and the dilution eats into the growth per share. At the same time the track ahead brightens: synergies of 0.8 billion DKK realized in 2025, a cumulative EBIT effect of around 5 billion expected in 2026 and the full target of 9 billion calculated for 2027, while the integration is 30 percent complete and the end date has been moved to the end of 2026.

The rule for the reader: an adjusted earnings figure is a working tool, not a truth — keep both lines visible across the quarters, exactly as [the quarterly report](/kurser/km-006-kvartalsrapporten)'s walkthrough of one-off items teaches. The cash flow confirmed it in 2025: adjusted free cash flow of 16.3 billion DKK against 5.6 billion in 2024, a reminder that working capital and integration pull in different directions in the income statement — [the cash flow analysis](/kurser/km-003-kassaflodesanalysen) and [capital tie-up](/kurser/ln-04-kapitalbindning-och-rorelsekapital) deepen precisely that mechanism.

## Valuation through the cycle — normalize EBIT first

Valuing logistics stocks on P/E at the peak year's earnings is the classic trap: when EBIT peaks, the multiple looks cheap precisely because the denominator is at its highest — one of [the P/E ratio's three betrayals](/kurser/km-009-pe). The craft is normalization: compute an average EBIT across a full cycle — for Maersk it spans pandemic boom, collapse, the Red Sea and normalization — and set [EV/EBIT](/kurser/km-010-evebit) against the normalized level, with net debt and equity visible ([what EV/EBITDA measures](/blogg/vad-ar-ev-ebitda)). The companies' own outlooks — DSV's range of 23.0–25.5 billion DKK EBIT before one-off items for 2026 — are in cyclical industries ranges, not promises. The moat in logistics is thin but not absent: network density, customer contracts and integration into customers' systems — how it is measured in numbers is covered in [the moat in numbers](/kurser/mt-03-vallgraven-i-siffror).

## Five points for reading the report

- **Volume against yield.** Split growth into units and price — a revenue increase driven solely by freight rates is cycle, not success.
- **Segment by segment.** Do not mix the road division's margins with sea and air freight's — DSV's three divisions carry three different economies.
- **Adjusted against reported.** Follow the one-off items across the quarters (DSV: 0.9 → 4.5 billion DKK) and ask when they level out.
- **Cash flow and capital tie-up.** Receivables and payment terms to subcontractors swing with freight rates — read [the balance sheet](/blogg/sa-laser-du-en-balansrakning-pa-15-minuter) alongside the earnings.
- **Capacity news outside the report.** Newbuild orders, reroutes and tariffs are the leading indicators of freight rates — [the sector analysis method](/kurser/se-16-sektoranalysens-metod) structures the track.

## The summary

- Three business models: the shipping line (capital intensive, high leverage), the forwarder (gross profit is the real revenue), contract logistics (stable volume, strict margin).
- The freight cycle in one line: Maersk EBIT 31 → 4 → 6.5 → 3.5 billion dollars 2022–2025; operating margin 37.8 → 6.5 percent.
- DSV 2025: revenue 247.3 billion DKK, gross margin 27.0 percent, EBIT before one-off items +21.8 percent — but reported profit −16.8 percent and unchanged EPS of 50.9 DKK: the acquisition's two sides in one report.
- Kuehne+Nagel's −24.9 percent shows the market beneath DSV's acquisition veil.
- Value normalized through the cycle; read volume and yield separately.

The continuation track: [The logistics sector](/kurser/se-04-logistiksektorn) and [Logistics and chains](/kurser/se-15-logistik) take the industry course by course, and [the complete guide to Swedish stock analysis](/blogg/komplett-guide-svensk-aktieanalys-2026) places the method in the whole.

_This is educational financial analysis, not investment advice._
